opus-5.5.text:
I think it was actually very valuable, although at the time it didn't always feel that way. When I started my PhD, computer vision was a very different field. You had to understand the image formation process, projective geometry, optimization, probabilistic graphical models, and a lot of hand-designed features. Each problem had its own carefully engineered pipeline. When deep learning arrived, many of those pipelines were replaced almost overnight, and a lot of people, including me, had to ask whether all those years were wasted.

Looking back, I don't think they were. The specific techniques, many of them, are no longer used directly. But the way of thinking stayed with me. Traditional vision trained you to ask, what is the structure of this problem? What is the physics behind how the pixels are generated? What assumptions am I making, and where do they break? That kind of first-principles thinking turns out to be very useful even when you are training large neural networks, because you still need to decide what data to use, what the model should represent, how to formulate the objective, and how to tell whether the result is actually correct or just looks correct.

For example, when I worked on generative models, image synthesis, and later video and world models, a lot of the intuition came from that older background: understanding geometry, consistency across views, how lighting and materials interact, and how 3D structure shows up in 2D images. Now we want models to understand the physical world, and those classical concepts come back in a new form. You may not write the equations by hand anymore, but knowing what the model should be capturing helps you design better systems and better evaluations.

There is also something about the mindset. In the pre-deep-learning era, progress was slow and incremental, so you learned patience and rigor. You had to really understand why something worked. When deep learning came, the field became very empirical and very fast. I think having both experiences is good: you can move quickly with large-scale learning, but you still keep the habit of asking why, and of respecting the structure of the problem.

So my view is that the foundation is less about the specific tools and more about the intuition and the discipline. The tools change every few years. The underlying questions, how do we perceive, represent, and simulate the world, those stay the same.

r001.rationale: The candidate says Liu had to understand a broad range of areas and that each problem used an engineered pipeline, but does not explain that traditional vision lacked reliably effective methods or that this lack forced him to learn those techniques.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it was a very valuable foundation, maybe more valuable than people assume today.

When I did my PhD at Maryland with Rama Chellappa, deep learning hadn't taken off yet. We were working with hand-designed features, probabilistic graphical models, Markov random fields, geometric methods, optimization. You had to really think about the structure of the problem. What is a camera actually doing? How does light interact with a surface? What makes two image patches similar? You couldn't just throw data at a network and hope it figured things out, because the networks weren't there yet. So you were forced to build intuition about the physical and statistical nature of images.

That intuition hasn't gone away. A lot of what I do now with generative models, with world models, with simulation for robotics, comes back to those questions. When you want a video model to understand physics, or when you want to render a scene consistently from multiple viewpoints, you are really dealing with geometry, with 3D structure, with the same things we studied in the classical era. The tools changed, the questions didn't.

There is also a mindset you get from that period. You learn to be skeptical, to ask why something works, to decompose a system and understand each piece. In the deep learning era it's easy to treat everything as a black box and just scale it. Scaling is powerful, I believe in it strongly, but knowing where the structure lives helps you decide what to scale and what to design. Many of the breakthroughs people admire, like diffusion models or neural rendering, came from people who understood the older theory and knew how to connect it to learning.

So I don't see it as wasted time at all. I was lucky to catch the transition. I had enough of the old world to understand the problems deeply, and I entered the new world early enough to help build it.

r001.rationale: The response lists several traditional techniques and says their absence of deep learning forced Liu to build intuition. It does not say traditional computer vision lacked reliably effective methods.

astra-6.text:
I think that foundation has been very valuable. In traditional computer vision, you had to think carefully about how an image is formed, what information you could extract from it, and what assumptions made a problem tractable. You couldn’t simply expect a model to learn everything from data.

Deep learning changed the tools dramatically, but many of the underlying questions stayed the same. How do you represent the world? How do you handle ambiguity? What constraints can help you recover something you can’t observe directly? That earlier training gives me a useful perspective on those questions.

At the same time, you have to be willing to let go of old approaches. I see the foundation as a way to ask better questions, rather than a reason to keep solving problems the same way.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes careful reasoning about image formation, assumptions, and constraints, but does not say that traditional vision lacked reliably effective methods or that this forced Liu to learn a broad range of techniques.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it gave me a very useful foundation. In traditional computer vision, we spent a lot of time thinking about how images are formed, what assumptions a method makes, and how to formulate a problem mathematically. You had to understand the structure of the problem before you could design a solution.

With deep learning, we can learn many things that we previously had to design by hand. But those fundamental questions are still there: What information is available in the image? Is the problem ambiguous? What constraints would help? That background gives me a way to reason about why a model works and where it might fail.

So I see the two as complementary. The tools have changed dramatically, but understanding the underlying problem remains very valuable.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes traditional computer vision as a useful foundation for reasoning about images and problems, but does not say that effective methods were lacking or that this forced Liu to learn a broad range of techniques.
